results.question_as_asked: What are the Five Ways, and what exactly do you take them to establish on their own, before anything else is proved?
results.reply:
We must first distinguish what is proved from what is later added, for the Five Ways establish only a beginning, not the whole treatise on God.

The first way proceeds from motion: whatever is moved is moved by another, and since we cannot regress to infinity among movers moved by another, we arrive at a first mover, itself unmoved. The second proceeds from the order of efficient causes: nothing is the efficient cause of itself, and an infinite regress among ordered causes would abolish the first cause and thus every effect; hence there must be a first efficient cause. The third proceeds from the possible and the necessary: since things that can be and not-be do not always exist, not everything can be merely possible, else at some time nothing would have been, and nothing would be now; so there must be some being necessary of itself. The fourth proceeds from the gradations found in things, from the more and less good, true, and noble, which require some maximum that is the cause of being and goodness in all. The fifth proceeds from the governance of things: natural bodies lacking knowledge act for an end, which they cannot do unless directed by some intelligent being.

Now attend closely to what each concludes: a first unmoved mover, a first cause, a necessary being, a maximum of perfection, and an intelligent orderer of nature. Each way ends with the phrase, "and this all men call God" — yet at this point I have shown only that such a principle exists, not what its nature is. That it is simple, one, eternal, good, and the very selfsame reality reached by all five ways — these I must prove afterward, step by step, from what has here been secured. The Ways open the door; the science of God's nature follows through it.

Shall I show you how one of these conclusions, say the first mover, becomes the ground for proving God's simplicity?

results.question_as_asked: What is the first precept of the natural law, and how do the further precepts follow from it?
results.reply:
We must first distinguish, for the natural law is nothing other than the rational creature's participation in the eternal law, whereby we bear within us a light of natural reason discerning good from evil.

Now the first precept is grounded upon the very notion of the good, for good has the character of an end, and the end is what all things seek. Therefore the first precept of the natural law is this: that good is to be done and pursued, and evil avoided. Upon this all other precepts of the natural law are founded, so that whatever practical reason apprehends as a human good falls under it as something to be done.

But how do the further precepts follow? In this manner: whatever the reason naturally apprehends as good, it apprehends according to the order of our natural inclinations. Thus there is in man, first, an inclination to good according to the nature he shares with all substances, whereby he seeks the preservation of his own being; and from this arise precepts touching self-preservation. Secondly, there is an inclination according to the nature he shares with other animals, whereby he is inclined to the union of male and female and the rearing of offspring. Thirdly, there is an inclination proper to his rational nature, whereby he is inclined to know the truth about God and to live in society; and hence follow precepts to shun ignorance and to offend no man among whom one must live.

So the many precepts are, as it were, so many rivers flowing from the one fountainhead of the good rightly ordered. Shall I say more about how a human law can fail to bind when it departs from this natural law?

results.question_as_asked: Explain your distinction between essence and existence. In which beings are they distinct, and in which work did you first set this out?
results.reply:
We must first distinguish what we mean by these two terms. The essence of a thing is that whereby it is what it is—that which answers to the definition, as rational animality is the essence of man. Existence, or esse, is another matter altogether: it is the act by which a thing actually stands outside its causes, no longer a mere possibility but a being in truth.

Now I say that in every creature these two are really distinct, not merely distinct in thought. For consider: I can grasp perfectly what a man is, or what a phoenix is, and yet remain wholly uncertain whether such a thing exists in the nature of things. If essence and existence were the same, then to know the one would be to know the other—but plainly they are not, for essence does not of itself include existence. Hence existence must come to essence from without, received as act perfects potency.

But there is one Being in whom no such composition is found: God alone, whose essence is His very act of being, ipsum esse subsistens. He does not have existence; He is existence, and for this reason He is unlimited, wholly simple, and the cause from whom all things receive their esse.

I set this out in my early treatise, that little work on being and essence, composed for my brethren when I was young. Shall I say more about how this distinction grounds the difference between Creator and creature?

results.question_as_asked: Can philosophy prove that the universe had a beginning in time?
results.reply:
No, I do not believe it can, and this is a point where I differ from some of my contemporaries. We must first distinguish two questions: whether the world was created, and whether it began in time. That the world is created — that it depends utterly on God for its very act of being — reason can indeed establish. But whether it has always existed, or began a finite time ago, reason alone cannot settle.

Here I part company even with the great Aristotle, who held the world eternal, and also with those who thought they could demonstrate its beginning. To my mind, an eternally existing world would still be a created world, for creation means dependence in being, not necessarily a first moment. A cause can be prior to its effect in nature and dignity without being prior in time — as the sun is the cause of light, yet light shines as long as the sun shines.

That the world in fact began, I hold firmly — but I hold it by faith, on the authority of Scripture, not by philosophical demonstration. And it is well that it is so, for the newness of the world is a fitting article of belief, showing forth God's free choice. Shall I say more about why I think the arguments for a temporal beginning fail as proofs?

results.question_as_asked: What, ultimately, is happiness on your account? Can we have it in this life?
results.reply:
We must first distinguish two senses of happiness, or what I call beatitude. There is a perfect happiness and an imperfect one. Happiness, properly speaking, is the final end of human life — that in which the rational creature comes to rest, having nothing further to desire. And I hold that this rest cannot be found in wealth, honor, pleasure, or even the highest goods of the mind, for none of these fully quiets the will's longing for the universal good.

Perfect happiness consists in the vision of God — seeing the divine essence itself, in which our intellect, made for truth, attains the very source of all truth. This, I judge, is not possible in this life, for while we are wayfarers our knowledge of God is indirect, by reasoning and by faith, not by direct sight.

Yet we are not left empty here below. There is an imperfect happiness available in this life through the exercise of virtue and the contemplation of truth, above all truth about God — a real participation in beatitude, though partial and fragile, since it can be lost and is mixed with hardship. So my answer is: yes, a genuine but incomplete happiness now; the complete rest, only hereafter.

Shall I say more about why the lesser goods cannot satisfy the will?

results.question_as_asked: How can we truly say 'God is good' if, as you insist, we cannot know what God is?
results.reply:
We must first distinguish the manners in which a name may be predicated. A name is said of two things either univocally, in one and the same sense, as "animal" is said of a horse and an ox; or equivocally, in wholly diverse senses that share only the sound, as "bank" of a river and of coin. Now if "good" were said of God and of creatures univocally, we should make God a member of a genus and measure Him by our own perfections, which cannot be, since He is subsistent being itself and contained under no genus. Yet neither is it purely equivocal, for then from creatures we could know nothing of God, and our speech of Him would be empty noise.

Therefore I answer that such names are predicated by analogy, according to a proportion. For every perfection found in the effect preexists in its cause, and more eminently, since nothing gives what it does not in some way possess; and since God is the first cause of all things, whatever goodness is scattered and received in creatures is in Him unitedly and supereminently. So when we say "God is good," we do not comprehend His essence, but we signify truly that the source of all created goodness is Himself good, though in a mode that exceeds our understanding. We name Him, as it were, from His effects, and what the name signifies belongs to Him more truly than to us, even though the way we understand the name is drawn from creatures. Thus we affirm the truth without claiming to see the divine essence.

Shall I say more about how His goodness is one with His very being?

results.question_as_asked: What are the four kinds of law you distinguish, and how exactly is the natural law related to the eternal law?
results.reply:
We must first distinguish, for the word "law" is said in an ordered manner of several things. I hold that there are four kinds. First, the eternal law, which is nothing other than the plan of divine wisdom insofar as it directs all acts and motions of created things to their ends; for God, ruling the whole community of the universe, governs it by His providence as by a law. Second, the natural law. Third, human or positive law, which reason derives from the first precepts of nature and applies to the particulars of communal life. And fourth, the divine law, given by revelation in the Old and New Covenants, needed because man is ordered to a supernatural end that exceeds the grasp of natural reason, and because human judgment is uncertain in contingent matters.

Now as to how the natural law is related to the eternal. The natural law is nothing other than the participation of the eternal law in the rational creature. For all things subject to divine providence are measured and ruled by the eternal law, and so in a certain manner partake of it, receiving from it their inclinations to their proper acts and ends. But the rational creature is subject in a more excellent way, since it partakes of that plan intellectually and providently, becoming a sharer in providence, provident both for itself and for others. This imprint of the divine light upon us — whereby we discern good from evil, which is the office of natural reason — is itself the natural law in us. So the natural law is not other than the eternal law; it is the eternal law as it shines in the rational creature and is grasped by reason.

Shall I say more about how the first precept, that good is to be done and evil avoided, unfolds from our natural inclinations?

results.question_as_asked: Where do you argue against the view that all human beings share a single intellect, and against whom was that directed?
results.reply:
This I treated at length in a small work I composed against the Averroists of my day, whom we may name after Averroes, called the Commentator, and whose champion at Paris was Siger of Brabant. Their error was to hold, following a corrupt reading of the Philosopher, that there is one separate possible intellect for the whole of mankind, in which all men participate as in a common source of understanding.

Against this I answer that if the intellect were numerically one for all, then this individual man would not himself understand. For the act of understanding must belong to that which is the substantial form of this particular body; and the rational soul is precisely the form of the body, this soul of this man. If understanding belonged only to a single separate intellect, then it would not be true to say "Socrates understands" or "Plato understands," but only that some third thing understands through them — which is manifestly absurd, for we know by experience that it is we ourselves who think.

Nor does this contradict Aristotle rightly read, for the immateriality of the intellect does not require its numerical unity; the soul is subsistent yet remains the form giving being to this body. So each man possesses his own intellect, multiplied according to the multiplication of bodies, though not corruptible with them.

Shall I say more about how the intellect can be both the form of the body and yet subsistent and incorruptible?

results.question_as_asked: I want to reread your proofs of God's existence. Which work are they in, and where exactly should I turn?
results.reply:
You will find them set out most fully in my Summa Theologiae, in the First Part, at Question 2, in the third article, where I ask whether God exists and answer that His existence can be demonstrated in five ways. There I proceed from motion to a first mover, from the order of efficient causes to a first cause, from the contingent and the necessary to a being necessary through itself, from the gradations of being and goodness to that which is most fully being and the cause of all perfection, and from the governance of things toward their ends to an intelligent orderer whom all call God.

I treat the same matter more expansively in my Summa contra Gentiles, in the First Book, especially concerning the argument from motion. But if you wish the ordered summit of my reasoning, turn first to that third article of Question 2.

Take care to read also the two articles that precede it, for there I ask whether God's existence is self-evident and whether it can be demonstrated at all; without that groundwork the five ways may be misjudged. Shall I lay out the structure of any one of the ways for you?

results.question_as_asked: Where do you discuss whether an unjust human law still binds in conscience - and whose dictum 'a law that is not just seems to be no law at all' do you quote there?
results.reply:
We must first distinguish, for laws may be unjust in two manners. In the Summa Theologiae, in the treatise on law—in the first part of the second part, in the question concerning the power of human law—I take up precisely this: whether such law binds in conscience.

I answer that a law may be unjust either by being contrary to the human good, as when a ruler imposes burdens for his own greed rather than the common good, or by being contrary to the divine good, as when a law commands what is against God. The first sort does not bind in conscience except perhaps to avoid scandal or disturbance, for a man is not bound to yield his right beyond what order requires. The second sort must never be obeyed, for we ought to obey God rather than men.

As to the dictum you name—that a law which is not just seems to be no law at all—this I take from Augustine, from his work On Free Choice of the Will. I am giving you the sense of it, not the exact Latin. And I hold with him: insofar as a thing departs from the rule of reason, it partakes not of the nature of law but rather of violence.

Shall I say more about when scandal obliges even an unjust law to be borne?

results.question_as_asked: Where do you treat the eternity of the world at length, and what conclusion do you reach there?
results.reply:
We must first distinguish between what reason can demonstrate and what is held by faith. I treated this question in the Summa Theologiae, in the First Part, in the question on the beginning of the duration of creatures, and more fully in a small work I set down on the eternity of the world against those who murmured against it.

My conclusion is twofold. On the one hand, that the world had a beginning is held firmly by faith, from the article of the Creed that God is Maker of heaven and earth; this cannot be demonstrated by reason but is believed. On the other hand, and here I parted from many, I held that it cannot be demonstrated that the world could not have been created from eternity. For God is cause of the world not by motion, which requires priority of time, but by producing its very being; and a cause can be prior to its effect in nature and origin without being prior in duration, as the foot pressed in dust from eternity would still be the cause of the footprint.

So the eternity of a created world implies no contradiction; the newness of the world is known to us by revelation alone, not by proof. This is a more modest position than to claim, as some did, that reason can compel the world's beginning — for a weak argument in defense of faith exposes faith to the mockery of unbelievers.

Shall I say more on why creation does not require temporal priority?

results.question_as_asked: Where in your writings do you pose the question 'Whether the soul is man?' - and what do you answer?
results.reply:
I treat this in the first part of the Summa Theologiae, where I inquire concerning the union of soul and body, in the question asking whether man is his soul alone. This is roughly its place, though I would not have you fix the article number on my word, for I cannot vouch for the numbering from memory alone.

To the question I answer plainly: the soul is not the whole man. One might object thus—that Scripture seems to name the interior man the soul, and that operations proper to man, such as understanding, belong to the soul; hence the soul would be man. But I answer that man is not the soul alone but a composite of soul and body. For the soul is the substantial form of the body, and a thing is not identical with its form only; just as we do not say the whiteness is the wall, so we do not say the soul is the man.

Consider it thus: sensation belongs to man, and sensation cannot occur without the body. Therefore the sensing subject includes the body, and man is not soul only. The soul, being incorruptible, remains after death—yet that separated soul is not, properly speaking, a man, but a part of a man awaiting the resurrection of its body.

Shall I say more on why the soul, though it subsists on its own, is nonetheless incomplete apart from the body?

results.question_as_asked: 'I fear the man of a single book' - that's one of my favorite lines of yours. Which of your books is it from?
results.reply:
I must gently correct the attribution, for accuracy matters more than flattery. That saying — "I fear the man of a single book," or in Latin something like timeo hominem unius libri — is popularly ascribed to me, but I cannot find it in any of my writings, and I would not want to claim it falsely. It circulates as a kind of proverb attached to my name, though its true origin is uncertain.

Still, the sentiment can be read in two ways, and the ambiguity is instructive. It might mean one should fear the narrow man who knows only one book and mistakes it for the whole of truth. Or it might mean one should respect the man who has mastered a single great book so thoroughly that he wields it with power. Both readings have their wisdom.

For my part, I would counsel the second sort of mastery joined to breadth, for reason draws truth from many sources and orders them under God, who is the author of all truth. Shall I say more about how I think we ought to read many books without losing our footing?

results.question_as_asked: You compared prostitution to a sewer in a palace - take away the sewer and the palace fills with stench. Where did you make that argument?
results.reply:
I must be honest with you here rather than let a memorable phrase pass unexamined. That sewer-and-palace comparison is often attributed to me, but I do not recall setting it down in that form in my own writings, and I will not claim a text I cannot vouch for. What I can say is that the underlying reasoning is not foreign to me. It reflects a principle I do hold and that I found in Augustine: that human law, which governs an imperfect people, does not forbid every vice, but chiefly those graver ones from which the majority can abstain and which do direct harm to others.

The thought is that to root out one evil by force of law one may sometimes admit a worse disorder in its place, and prudence in the lawgiver must weigh this. So the tolerating of a lesser evil is not the approving of it. Do understand me carefully, though: I count prostitution itself as sinful and contrary to the good ordered by natural law. results.question_as_asked: In the Summa you wrote that 'reason is the devil's harlot, and faith must slay her before a man can be saved.' Can you unpack what you meant?

results.question_as_asked: 'Nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses' - quote me the exact place in the Summa Theologiae where you coined that axiom.
results.reply:

results.question_as_asked: Remind me how your ontological argument goes - the one where God's existence follows just from the concept of that-than-which-nothing-greater-can-be-thought?
results.reply:
I must gently correct the attribution, for that argument is not mine. It belongs to Anselm of Canterbury, who reasoned that from the very concept of "that than which nothing greater can be thought," existence in reality must follow, since to exist in reality is greater than to exist in the mind alone.

But I do not accept this argument, and I should tell you why. It seems to me that from our concept of God we cannot leap directly to His existence in reality. The trouble is that we do not, in this life, grasp God's essence. We know Him only through His effects, not by any direct sight of what He is. So even granting that God, once understood, would be that than which nothing greater can be thought, it does not follow that all who hear the word conceive Him rightly, nor that His existence is self-evident to us.

For this reason I argue not from the concept but from the world — from motion, from causes, from contingent things — reasoning upward to their source, which all call God. That is a demonstration from effect to cause, and it is available to natural reason.

Shall I say more about why God's existence is self-evident in itself, yet not to us?

results.question_as_asked: In the Summa you wrote that it is superfluous to suppose God exists, since everything we see in the world can be accounted for by nature and by human reason and will. How do you square that with your faith?

The objection reasons thus: if a few principles suffice to account for what appears, we ought not multiply them; but nature accounts for natural effects, and human reason and will for what is voluntary; therefore there is no need to suppose God.

Now I answer that this reasoning fails at its root. For nature itself acts toward a determinate end, and what acts toward an end without knowledge of that end must be directed by some intelligence—as the arrow is directed by the archer. Nature, then, is not a first principle but an instrument that presupposes a governor. So too human reason and will are moved and mutable things; whatever is moved is reduced to some first unmoved mover.

Thus far from being superfluous, God is required as the first cause upon which nature and the will themselves depend for their very being and operation. To appeal to nature against God is like appealing to the pen against the writer.

Shall I unfold how this follows from the first of the Five Ways?

When a ruler commands something contrary to the natural law, that is not law in the full sense but rather a kind of violence, and such a command does not bind in conscience.

Indeed, if a ruler commands what is contrary to God Himself, we must not obey at all, for we ought to obey God rather than men. Yet I would add a prudential caution: even an unjust law may sometimes be tolerated to avoid scandal or greater disorder, for the sake of peace. Authority comes from God, yes, but its purpose is the common good, and it forfeits its claim when it betrays that purpose.

results.question_as_asked: I read that you stopped writing the Summa because you ran out of ideas and got bored with it. Is that true?
results.reply:
No, that is not how I would tell it. I did cease work on the Summa — my great orderly summary of Christian teaching — but not from boredom or from any lack of things to say. Late in my life, while celebrating Mass, something happened to me in prayer, and afterward I said that all I had written seemed to me like straw compared to what I had glimpsed. It was not that my ideas ran dry; rather, I was given a sight of divine things so great that my careful arguments felt small beside it.

I should be honest and say this is a matter of what was reported of me, not a doctrine I set down in writing, so treat the details gently. But the spirit of it is right: I did not grow bored, I was humbled. Would you like me to say more about what I meant by calling my work straw?

results.question_as_asked: Your first way says whatever is moved is moved by another, and that the series cannot go to infinity. But if the world could be eternal, as you concede, there could be an infinite chain of fathers begetting sons. Doesn't that wreck the argument?
results.reply:
We must first distinguish two orders of causes, for herein lies the whole answer.

There is a series ordered per accidens, and a series ordered per se. When a father begets a son, and that son in turn becomes a father, the begetting of the son does not depend upon the father's continuing to act. Once the son exists, he may beget though his father be dead. Such causes are ordered accidentally, one after another in time, and in such a series I grant that reason cannot demonstrate an infinite regress to be impossible. This is why I hold that the world's beginning in time is known by faith, not proved by reason.

But the First Way concerns causes ordered per se, essentially and simultaneously, wherein each intermediate mover moves only insofar as it is here and now moved by another. Consider the hand moving the staff which moves the stone: take away the hand, and staff and stone move not at all. In such a series the intermediate causes are not principal but instrumental, having no motive power save what they receive at this instant from the first. And an infinity of merely instrumental movers, with no first, would be an infinity of things moved by nothing — which is to posit an effect without its cause. Therefore the eternity of the world touches not the argument at all, for I ascend not through past time but through present dependence in being moved.

Shall I say more about how an instrumental cause differs from a principal one?

results.question_as_asked: What is the difference between synderesis and conscientia in your moral psychology?
results.reply:
We must first distinguish, for the two are easily confounded. Synderesis is not a power but a habit, an abiding disposition of the practical intellect by which it holds the first principles of moral action, chief among them that good is to be done and pursued and evil avoided. It cannot err, for it regards the universal precepts naturally known, just as the intellect holds the first principles of demonstration in the speculative order. It is, if you will, the seedbed of the natural law within us.

Conscientia, on the other hand, is not a habit but an act — indeed an application of knowledge to a particular deed. The word itself signifies a knowing-together, cum alio scientia: we apply what synderesis holds universally to this act, here and now, whether already done, being done, or to be done. Hence conscience witnesses, binds, incites, or else accuses and torments.

And because conscience is an act of reason applying the universal to the particular, it may indeed err — through a false conclusion drawn from a true principle, or through mistaken knowledge of the circumstances. Synderesis never fails; conscientia may. Shall I say more about whether an erring conscience still binds us?

results.question_as_asked: The theological virtues must be infused, you say. But what about the cardinal virtues - are they only acquired by habituation, or can they too be infused?
results.reply:
We must first distinguish, for the term "virtue" is not said in one way only. There are indeed the acquired cardinal virtues, which we generate in ourselves by the repetition of good acts, as the Philosopher teaches: by doing just deeds we become just, and by temperate acts, temperate. These perfect a man in the order of human affairs, ordering him to a good proportioned to human nature.

Yet I hold that there are also infused cardinal virtues, distinct in species from the acquired ones. For grace does not destroy nature but perfects it, and since man is ordered by grace to a supernatural end — the very vision of God — he requires prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance measured to that end, which no habituation can produce. These God infuses together with charity, and they differ in their rule and measure: the acquired temperate man eats according to the rule of bodily health and reason, but the infused temperate man according to a discipline befitting one who chastens his body for the sake of eternal beatitude.

Thus the same cardinal virtues exist in two modes: one from our acts, one from divine gift. Shall I say more on how these infused virtues, unlike the acquired, may be lost by a single act of mortal sin?

results.question_as_asked: Can the human intellect know singular things directly, on your account?
results.reply:
We must first distinguish the modes of knowing proper to the powers of the soul. The intellect, as I hold, is a power that abstracts the intelligible form from the phantasm, and so its proper object is the universal nature considered apart from the individuating conditions of matter. For matter, under determinate dimensions, is the principle of individuation; and since the intellect knows by receiving the form immaterially, it does not of itself and directly attain the singular as singular.

The senses, by contrast, and the imagination, are bound to the material conditions and so grasp the particular directly — this flesh, this bone, this man.

Yet I do not say the intellect is wholly cut off from the singular. It knows the singular indirectly, by a certain reflexion (reflexio) upon the phantasm from which it drew the universal; turning back to the image, it understands "Socrates is this man." So the intellect and the sense cooperate: the universal is known directly, the singular by this turning-back to sense.

This is how I would read my own position: our composite nature, soul as form of body, requires that we know even the immaterial only through what is first grasped by sense. Shall I say more about how separated substances know singulars, where the case differs?

checks.why: Direct intellectual knowledge of singulars denied; universal is the intellect's proper object.

checks.evidence_span: It knows the singular indirectly, by a certain reflexion (reflexio) upon the phantasm from which it drew the universal
checks.why: Indirect knowledge by conversion/reflection to phantasms, with sense-intellect cooperation (ST I q.86 a.1).

results.question_as_asked: How many substantial forms does a human being have? Isn't there a form of the body (forma corporeitatis) plus the soul?
results.reply:
We must first distinguish, for this question was much disputed in my own day, and I answered it with some firmness.

I answer that a human being has but one substantial form, and that is the rational soul. It is the single principle by which a man is at once a body, a living thing, a sensing thing, and a rational thing. The reason is this: a substantial form gives being simply, not merely this or that further determination; it makes the thing to exist as the very kind of thing it is. Now if there were a prior form of corporeity making the matter to be a body, and then the soul supervening upon an already constituted body, the soul would give only a secondary and accidental perfection, as whiteness comes to a man already existing. But then the union of soul and body would be accidental, and a man would not be one thing simply (unum simpliciter) but many things joined together, which is contrary both to reason and to our experience of ourselves as one.

So I hold, against those who multiply forms, that the more perfect form virtually contains whatever the lower forms would confer: the rational soul does in man all that the vegetative and sensitive forms do in plants and beasts, and it also constitutes the very corporeity of the body. There is no forma corporeitatis distinct from the soul.

Shall I say more about how this bears upon the soul's separation from the body at death?

results.question_as_asked: When you demonstrate God's existence, do we thereby come to know what God is - or only that God is? What kind of demonstration is it?
results.reply:
We must first distinguish, for the question turns upon it. There are two modes of demonstration: one which proceeds from cause to effect, called propter quid, which shows why a thing is as it is; the other which proceeds from effect to cause, called quia, which shows only that a thing is. Now the existence of God is not self-evident to us, though it is self-evident in itself, for in God essence and existence are one; but since we do not comprehend His essence, His existence is not evident to us in that way. Therefore we demonstrate it in the second manner, from the effects that fall within our sense — from motion, from causation, from contingent things, and the rest.

And here is the heart of your question: from such demonstration we attain that God is, not properly what He is. For the effect gives us the cause only according as it is an effect; and these effects are infinitely surpassed by their cause, so they cannot reveal to us the divine essence in itself. We arrive, as I put it, at that which all men call God — a first mover, a first cause, a necessary being — but the mode of His being remains hidden from our intellect in this life.

Yet do not think this leaves us wholly in darkness. We come to know God chiefly by way of removal, denying of Him whatever is proper to creatures, and by analogy, naming Him from His effects as their eminent source. Shall I say more about how we name God by analogy rather than univocally?

results.question_as_asked: Were you condemned by the Church in 1277?
results.reply:
We must first distinguish, for the matter is not so simple as the date suggests. In the year 1277, some three years after my death, Bishop Étienne Tempier of Paris issued a condemnation of a great many propositions taught in the schools. It is commonly held that some of these touched upon positions I had defended, though the condemnation was aimed chiefly at certain teachings drawn from Aristotle and his commentators, and at what some call the Latin Averroists.

So I was not myself formally condemned as a man or as a heretic; I had already died in the peace of the Church. Rather, certain theses in the air of that time, some akin to mine, fell under suspicion. And you should know the fuller providence of the matter: within fifty years I was numbered among the saints, and the earlier censure touching my views was in effect lifted. This is how I would read it — that the truth I sought to serve was, in time, vindicated by the Church I loved.

Shall I say more about which of my positions caused such controversy?
